advances: The restricted original cubic-moment statement is true, with the absolute constant \(\kappa=2^{-22}\). The proof bounds the actual mass of every containing halfspace on a set having positive probability under the complete original sampling law. It uses points one integer height above their column entrance. A downward-tilting halfspace either contains many distinct neighbors at the entrance height or contains endpoints from almost every sufficiently late inverse-path pair. This mechanism uses different original heights from the symmetric reflection kernel centered at the sampled full index.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The rooted-tree support, forward blocks, inverse reconstruction, and level counts are used from accepted fact 032423921efad6c8. The exact log-affine height support, entrance counts, and total-mass bound are used from accepted fact 604889294a17d7df. The complete-continuation census, actual-halfspace argument, probability estimate, and cubic-moment bound are proved here.
proof:
Let \(\nu=\sum_{\mathbf I\in\widehat A}w_{\mathbf I}\delta_{\mathbf I}\), and let \(h_\nu(\mathbf I)=W\tau_p(\mathbf I)\). Thus \(h_\nu\) is the actual unnormalized depth of the original atomic measure, with every containing closed halfspace allowed. Write \(H_j=\sum_{r=1}^{j}1/r\) for harmonic numbers and \(\eta=1-2^{-m}\binom m{m/2}\), exactly as in accepted facts 032423921efad6c8 and 604889294a17d7df. We use from these facts the exact level counts, inverse-pair reconstruction, and bounds
$$
\eta^Q>\frac34,
\qquad
\frac W{2^N}\le1+\frac{H_k-H_7}{8}.
$$
The first bound also follows directly from their estimate \(1-\eta<1/(Q+1)^2\) and Bernoulli's inequality. No two-point reflection moment lower bound is assumed.

First suppose \(k\ge2^{16}\), and put \(u=\lfloor\sqrt{k}\rfloor\) and \(v=2u\). Thus \(u\ge256\), \(8\le u<v\le k\), and \(\log k\ge16\log2>32/3>9\). Here and below logarithms are natural; \(\log2>2/3\) follows, for example, by applying strict convexity of \(1/x\) to its integral on \([1,2]\).

For each tree level \(s\), call a base point \(j\in A_{m,Q}\) of level \(s\) complete if its inverse reconstruction in 032423921efad6c8 succeeds all the way from level \(s\) to level \(Q\). The number of complete points at each fixed level \(s\) is exactly \(2^n\eta^Q\). To check this count, first specify the \(s\) successive forward source blocks in \(D_m\), which determine the first \(s\) selected children. In the center \(j\), the selected zero in each such block has become two. Then specify the \(Q-s\) successive inverse blocks in \(\operatorname{im}F_m\), which determine the remaining selected children. These \(Q\) blocks are disjoint, their local patterns each have \(|D_m|=|\operatorname{im}F_m|=2^m\eta\) choices, and all other Boolean coordinates are free. The construction is injective and is reversed by the forward prefix and inverse reconstruction. Its count is therefore \(|D_m|^Q2^{n-mQ}=2^n\eta^Q\).

Define the actual original sampling subset
$$
\mathcal G
=\lbrace (j,a_s+1):
 j\in A_{m,Q}\text{ is complete of level }s,
 \quad 8\le a_s\le u\rbrace.
$$
Every such height is one of the original integer heights in its column, since \(a_s+1\le u+1\le k\). We shall prove \(h_\nu(\mathbf I)\ge(\log k)/128\) for every \(\mathbf I\in\mathcal G\).

Fix \(\mathbf I=(j,h)\in\mathcal G\), let \(s=\operatorname{level}(j)\), and put \(a=a_s\), so \(h=a+1\) and \(8\le a\le u\). Denote its full inverse continuation by \(u_{s+1},\ldots,u_Q\). These are the canonical tree coordinates of the accepted reconstruction, with \(j_{u_r}=1\). Set \(V_r=\sum_{\ell=s+1}^{r}e_{u_\ell}\) for \(s<r\le Q\). The reconstruction proves that \(j-V_r\) is a base point of level \(s\), \(j+V_r\) is a base point of level \(r\), and these are the unique reconstructed unordered pair for upper level \(r\).

There is a second family of actual base points useful here: \(j-e_{u_r}\in A_{m,Q}\) has level \(s\) for every \(r>s\). Indeed, replacing that one coordinate equal to one by zero does not alter any of the first \(s\) forward blocks or their selected coordinates equal to two. Its Boolean source still takes the same first \(s\) steps. Consequently the distinct original indices \((j-e_{u_r},a)\), all of weight \(2^{-a}\), belong to \(\widehat A\).

Take any proper closed halfspace through \(\mathbf I\), and write it as
$$
H=\lbrace (z,t):
 c^{\mathsf T}(z-j)+b(t-h)\ge0\rbrace,
\qquad (c,b)\ne(0,0).
$$
Every containing proper closed halfspace contains a parallel one through \(\mathbf I\), so it suffices to prove the required mass bound for these halfspaces. The whole-space case is immediate.

The total original weight available from one reconstructed endpoint at the entrance height of each level with entrance at least \(v\) is
$$
T=\sum_{\substack{s<r\le Q\\a_r\ge v}}2^{-a_r}
 =\sum_{\ell=v}^{k}b_\ell2^{-\ell}.
$$
The equality holds because \(a_s\le u<v\). The floor inequality and elementary harmonic estimates give
$$
\begin{aligned}
T
&\ge\frac{H_k-H_{v-1}}8-2^{1-v}\\
&\ge\frac18\log\frac{k+1}{v}-2^{1-v}\\
&\ge\frac{\log k}{16}-\frac{\log2}{8}-2^{1-v}
 \ge\frac{\log k}{32}.
\end{aligned}
$$
For the last bound, \(\log k>32/3\), \(\log2<1\), and \(v\ge512\) suffice.

If \(b\ge0\), then for every \(r\) occurring in \(T\), both original indices \((j-V_r,a_r)\) and \((j+V_r,a_r)\) exist, and \(a_r\ge v>h\). Their two values in the halfspace inequality are \(\pm c^{\mathsf T}V_r+b(a_r-h)\). At least one is nonnegative. The chosen endpoints are distinct as \(r\) varies: the lower endpoints have different vectors \(V_r\), the upper endpoints have different tree levels, and a lower endpoint of level \(s\) cannot be an upper endpoint of larger level. Hence \(\nu(H)\ge T\ge(\log k)/32\).

Suppose instead \(b<0\), and write \(\beta=-b>0\). Call an index \(r\in\lbrace s+1,\ldots,Q\rbrace\) bad if \(c_{u_r}\le\beta\), and let \(L\) be the number of bad indices. For every bad index the original neighbor at the lower entrance height satisfies
$$
c^{\mathsf T}(-e_{u_r})+b(a-h)
=\beta-c_{u_r}\ge0.
$$
Thus \(\nu(H)\ge L2^{-a}\). If \(L\ge2^a(\log k)/128\), this proves the desired lower bound.

It remains to consider \(L<2^a(\log k)/128\). Define the normalized partial sums \(S_r=\beta^{-1}c^{\mathsf T}V_r\). Between bad indices these sums have consecutive increments strictly greater than one. Each maximal run of nonbad indices therefore contains at most \(2k+1\) partial sums in \([-k,k]\). There are at most \(L+1\) such runs; also count the at most \(L\) bad indices themselves. Consequently
$$
\left|\lbrace r:s<r\le Q,\ |S_r|\le k\rbrace\right|
\le(2k+2)(L+1)
\le4k\,2^u\log k.
$$
The last bound uses \(a\le u\), \(k\ge1\), and \(L+1\le2^u\log k\).

For \(a_r\ge v\) and \(|S_r|>k\), at least one of the same two original endpoints at height \(a_r\) belongs to \(H\): its halfspace value is \(\beta(|S_r|-(a_r-h))>0\), because \(a_r-h\le k\). At worst discard all the indices with \(|S_r|\le k\). Each discarded index with \(a_r\ge v\) costs at most \(2^{-v}\) from \(T\). The same endpoint distinctness argument therefore gives
$$
\nu(H)
\ge T-4k\,2^u\log k\,2^{-v}
 =T-4k\,2^{-u}\log k
\ge\frac{\log k}{64}.
$$
Here \(2^u\ge256k\): since \(k<(u+1)^2\), it suffices to note that \(2^u/(u+1)^2\) is increasing for integers \(u\ge2\), and \(2^{256}>256\cdot257^2\). This proves the final loss bound \(4k2^{-u}\log k\le(\log k)/64\).

All cases prove, uniformly over every original containing closed halfspace,
$$
h_\nu(\mathbf I)\ge\frac{\log k}{128}
\qquad(\mathbf I\in\mathcal G).
$$
The use of selected actual neighbors and endpoints only lower-bounds the mass of the full original halfspace. No replacement probability law or conditioned depth has been introduced.

It remains to check the probability of \(\mathcal G\) under the original law. Put \(U=\sum_{\ell=8}^{u}b_\ell2^{-\ell}\). Since \(H_u\ge\log(u+1)\ge(\log k)/2\),
$$
U\ge\frac{H_u-H_7}{8}-\frac1{128}
\ge\frac{\log k}{16}-\frac{H_7}{8}-\frac1{128}
\ge\frac{\log k}{32}.
$$
For the last bound, use \(H_7=363/140<13/5\), hence \(H_7/8+1/128<1/3\), while \((\log k)/32>1/3\). The exact complete-point count gives
$$
\nu(\mathcal G)=2^{n-1}\eta^Q U
\ge\frac3{256}\,2^n\log k.
$$
Also the accepted upper bound for \(W\), together with \(H_k\le1+\log k\), gives
$$
W\le2^n\frac{9+\log k}{4}
\le2^{n-1}\log k
=2^{N-2}\log k,
$$
because \(\log k>9\). Therefore
$$
\frac{\nu(\mathcal G)}W\ge\frac3{128},
\qquad
\tau_p(\mathbf I)=\frac{h_\nu(\mathbf I)}W
\ge\frac{2^{-N}}{32}
\quad(\mathbf I\in\mathcal G).
$$
Using this subset only to lower-bound the expectation under the unchanged original law proves
$$
\sum_{\mathbf I\in\widehat A}p_{\mathbf I}\tau_p(\mathbf I)^3
\ge\frac3{128}\left(\frac{2^{-N}}{32}\right)^3
=3\cdot2^{-22}8^{-N}.
$$

Finally let \(8\le k<2^{16}\). All \(2^n\) Boolean base points at height zero belong to \(\widehat A\) and have original weight one. Every closed halfspace containing such a point has weight at least one, so its normalized depth is at least \(1/W\). Moreover,
$$
\frac W{2^N}\le1+\frac{H_k-H_7}{8}
\le1+\frac{1+\log k}{8}<4,
$$
since \(\log k<16\log2<16\). Thus these original atoms alone give
$$
\sum_{\mathbf I\in\widehat A}p_{\mathbf I}\tau_p(\mathbf I)^3
\ge\frac{2^n}{W^4}
>\frac{2^{N-1}}{(4\cdot2^N)^4}
=2^{-9}8^{-N}
\ge2^{-22}8^{-N}.
$$
This completes the proof for every \(k\ge8\), with every original column height and the original normalization retained.
statement:
For every integer \(k\ge8\), use exactly the log-affine specialization \(\rho_t=2^{-t}\) in accepted fact 604889294a17d7df, with the rooted-tree construction of accepted fact 032423921efad6c8. Thus \(b_\ell=0\) for \(1\le\ell<8\), \(b_\ell=\lfloor2^\ell/(8\ell)\rfloor\) for \(8\le\ell\le k\), \(Q_\ell=\sum_{r=1}^{\ell}b_r\), \(Q=Q_k\), \(m=2(Q+1)^4\), \(n=\sum_{r=1}^{Q}m^r\), and \(N=n+1\). The entrance heights are \(a_0=0\) and \(a_s=\ell\) when \(Q_{\ell-1}<s\le Q_\ell\). Retain all the exact objects \(D_m,F_m,A_{m,Q},P_{m,Q},\widehat P,\widehat A\) of these predecessors, for any allowed symmetric saturated chain partition. In particular,
$$
\widehat A
=\lbrace (z,t):z\in A_{m,Q},\quad
 a_{\operatorname{level}(z)}\le t\le k,\quad t\in\mathbb Z\rbrace.
$$
Put \(w_{(z,t)}=2^{-t}\) at every point of \(\widehat A\), put all other lattice weights equal to zero, and set \(W=\sum_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf I}\) and \(p_{\mathbf I}=w_{\mathbf I}/W\). For every \(\mathbf I\in\widehat A\), define its original halfspace depth by
$$
\tau_p(\mathbf I)
=\inf\left\lbrace
\sum_{\mathbf J\in H\cap\widehat A}p_{\mathbf J}:
H\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ is a closed halfspace containing }\mathbf I
\right\rbrace.
$$
Then, with the complete original support, columns, weights, and sampling law,
$$
\sum_{\mathbf I\in\widehat A}p_{\mathbf I}\tau_p(\mathbf I)^3
\ge 2^{-22}8^{-N}.
$$
More precisely, if \(k\ge2^{16}\), there is an explicitly specified subset \(\mathcal G\subseteq\widehat A\) with \(\sum_{\mathbf I\in\mathcal G}p_{\mathbf I}\ge3/128\) and \(\tau_p(\mathbf I)\ge 2^{-N}/32\) at every \(\mathbf I\in\mathcal G\).
